(CNN)  -- Mauricio Funes was inaugurated Monday as El Salvador's president, promising to work for the nation's poor and disadvantaged. El Salvador's new president, Mauricio Funes, takes power Monday after his inauguration in San Salvador. Funes, elected March 15, is a member of a political party that waged guerrilla war against the government 17 years ago. He is El Salvador's first leftist president. "The Salvadoran public asked for a change, and that change begins now," Funes said in an inauguration speech before an audience that included Latin American leaders and U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. Funes, a member of the FMLN party, won a narrow victory over the ARENA party's Rodrigo Avila. Funes' victory ended a 20-year hold on the presidency by the right-leaning ARENA. With Funes' win, El Salvador joined other Latin American countries that have elected leftist leaders in recent years -- Venezuela, Bolivia, Nicaragua, Argentina, Honduras, Guatemala, Ecuador and Brazil. The FMLN, which is the Spanish acronym for the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front, was formed in 1980 as an umbrella group for five leftist guerilla organizations fighting a U.S.-backed military dictatorship. The guerrillas and the government signed a peace pact in 1992, and the FMLN became a legitimate political party. By some estimates, 75,000 Salvadorans died during the war. The new president will find "a country that still retains a lot of bitterness, a lot of division," Peter Hakim, president of the Washington-based Inter-American Dialogue policy institute, said before the election. "This country is completely divided," ARENA party official Adolfo Torres said on CNN affiliate TCS TV on election night. Funes acknowledged that division Monday, promising to "create a country without hate and without resentment." He also seemed to acknowledge the difficulties ahead, saying, "We don't have the right to make mistakes." Despite a dire economy, Funes promised an ambitious social program that would include construction of 11,000 homes, scholarships for children ages 6 to 18 and improvement in delivery of water, electricity and sanitary services to 32 poor municipalities. He may be hard-pressed to follow through, some analysts said. "Once Funes assumes office on 1 June, his government will face major challenges to boost the economy, cut government expenditures to trim the fiscal deficit and maintain support to the poor, who are being hit hardest by the economic downturn," analyst Heather Berkman wrote in a report last week for the Eurasia Group consulting firm. "Cutting expenditures and reducing the deficit will be the most important challenges," Berkman wrote, adding that to "do this, the Funes administration plans to cut government spending and eliminate redundant presidential commissions; retarget propane subsidies (and perhaps eventually eliminate them); and propose a number of new taxes on alcoholic beverages, tobacco and new vehicles." Funes campaigned on a platform of fiscal reform that aims to increase the government's tax take incrementally, Berkman said. Funes did not offer any details Monday, speaking instead in general terms of the El Salvador he would like to see under his five-year administration. He will not, Funes said, "govern for a few or be complacent to corruption." Funes, a former freelance journalist for CNN en Español, noted in particular that his administration will fight organized crime and narcotraffickers. "In this government," he said, "those who have merit will be compensated and those who are guilty will be punished."

(CNN) — Mauricio Funes was inaugurated Monday as president of El Salvador, pledging to work on behalf of the nation’s poor and disadvantaged.

El Salvador’s new president, Mauricio Funes, assumed office Monday following his inauguration in San Salvador. Elected on March 15, Funes belongs to a political party that waged guerrilla war against the government 17 years ago. He is El Salvador’s first leftist president.

“The Salvadoran public asked for a change, and that change begins now,” Funes said in an inaugural address before an audience that included Latin American leaders and U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton.

Funes, a member of the FMLN party, won a narrow victory over Rodrigo Avila of the ARENA party. His win ended ARENA’s 20-year hold on the presidency.

With Funes’ election, El Salvador joined a number of other Latin American countries that have chosen leftist leaders in recent years, including Venezuela, Bolivia, Nicaragua, Argentina, Honduras, Guatemala, Ecuador and Brazil.

The FMLN, the Spanish acronym for the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front, was formed in 1980 as an umbrella organization for five leftist guerrilla groups fighting a U.S.-backed military dictatorship. The guerrillas and the government signed a peace agreement in 1992, after which the FMLN became a legitimate political party. By some estimates, 75,000 Salvadorans died during the war.

The new president will inherit “a country that still retains a lot of bitterness, a lot of division,” Peter Hakim, president of the Washington-based Inter-American Dialogue policy institute, said before the election.

“This country is completely divided,” ARENA party official Adolfo Torres said on CNN affiliate TCS TV on election night.

Funes acknowledged that division Monday, pledging to “create a country without hate and without resentment.” He also appeared to recognize the difficulties ahead, saying, “We don’t have the right to make mistakes.”

Despite a dire economy, Funes promised an ambitious social program that would include the construction of 11,000 homes, scholarships for children ages 6 to 18, and improvements in the delivery of water, electricity and sanitation services to 32 poor municipalities.

Some analysts said he may be hard-pressed to fulfill those commitments.

“Once Funes assumes office on 1 June, his government will face major challenges to boost the economy, cut government expenditures to trim the fiscal deficit and maintain support to the poor, who are being hit hardest by the economic downturn,” analyst Heather Berkman wrote in a report last week for the Eurasia Group consulting firm.

“Cutting expenditures and reducing the deficit will be the most important challenges,” Berkman wrote, adding that, to “do this, the Funes administration plans to cut government spending and eliminate redundant presidential commissions; retarget propane subsidies (and perhaps eventually eliminate them); and propose a number of new taxes on alcoholic beverages, tobacco and new vehicles.”

Funes campaigned on a platform of fiscal reform intended to increase the government’s tax revenue incrementally, Berkman said.

Funes offered no details Monday, speaking instead in broad terms about the El Salvador he hopes to shape during his five-year administration. He said he would not “govern for a few or be complacent to corruption.”

Funes, a former freelance journalist for CNN en Español, emphasized in particular that his administration would combat organized crime and narcotraffickers.

“In this government,” he said, “those who have merit will be compensated and those who are guilty will be punished.”

(CNN) — Mauricio Funes took the oath of office Monday as president of El Salvador, pledging to serve the country’s poor and marginalized citizens.

Funes assumed power in San Salvador following his inauguration. He had been elected on March 15 and belongs to a party that, 17 years earlier, had fought the Salvadoran government as a guerrilla movement. He is the first left-wing president in El Salvador’s history.

“The Salvadoran public asked for a change, and that change begins now,” Funes said during his inaugural address, delivered before a crowd that included leaders from Latin America as well as U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton.

A member of the FMLN party, Funes narrowly defeated Rodrigo Avila of the ARENA party. His election brought an end to two decades of presidential control by the right-leaning ARENA party. With his victory, El Salvador became part of a broader regional trend in which several Latin American nations have chosen leftist presidents in recent years, including Venezuela, Bolivia, Nicaragua, Argentina, Honduras, Guatemala, Ecuador and Brazil.

FMLN stands in Spanish for the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front. The organization was created in 1980 as a coalition of five leftist guerrilla groups that were battling a U.S.-supported military dictatorship. In 1992, the rebels and the government reached a peace agreement, after which the FMLN became a legal political party. According to some estimates, the civil war claimed the lives of 75,000 Salvadorans.

Before the election, Peter Hakim, president of the Washington-based Inter-American Dialogue policy institute, said the incoming president would inherit “a country that still retains a lot of bitterness, a lot of division.”

On election night, ARENA official Adolfo Torres told CNN affiliate TCS TV, “This country is completely divided.”

Funes addressed that rift on Monday, vowing to “create a country without hate and without resentment.” He also appeared to recognize the scale of the challenges facing his government, saying, “We don’t have the right to make mistakes.”

Even with the economy in poor condition, Funes laid out an ambitious social agenda. His proposals included building 11,000 houses, providing scholarships for children between the ages of 6 and 18, and improving access to water, electricity and sanitation services in 32 impoverished municipalities.

Some analysts, however, questioned whether he would be able to fulfill those promises.

“Once Funes assumes office on 1 June, his government will face major challenges to boost the economy, cut government expenditures to trim the fiscal deficit and maintain support to the poor, who are being hit hardest by the economic downturn,” analyst Heather Berkman wrote the previous week in a report for the consulting firm Eurasia Group.

Berkman said the most pressing tasks would be lowering public spending and shrinking the deficit. She wrote that, to achieve this, the Funes government intended to reduce state spending, abolish unnecessary presidential commissions, redirect propane subsidies and possibly remove them later, and seek new taxes on alcoholic drinks, tobacco and new vehicles.

According to Berkman, Funes ran on a fiscal reform agenda designed to gradually raise the amount of tax revenue collected by the government.

In his Monday remarks, Funes did not provide specifics, choosing instead to speak broadly about the kind of El Salvador he hoped to shape during his five-year term. He said he would not “govern for a few or be complacent to corruption.”

Funes, who previously worked as a freelance journalist for CNN en Español, emphasized that his administration would take on organized crime and drug traffickers.

“In this government,” he said, “those who have merit will be compensated and those who are guilty will be punished.”

**SAN SALVADOR, El Salvador —** Mauricio Funes was sworn in Monday as president of El Salvador, ending two decades of conservative rule and bringing the former guerrilla movement that fought the country’s bloody civil war into power through the ballot box for the first time.

Funes, a former television journalist and the candidate of the leftist Farabundo Martí National Liberation Front, or FMLN, took the oath of office in a ceremony attended by regional leaders, diplomats and thousands of supporters who celebrated what many described as a historic political shift.

“I will govern for all Salvadorans,” Funes said in his inaugural address, promising a government rooted in reconciliation, transparency and social inclusion. “The time has come to build a country that offers opportunities, dignity and hope.”

Funes’ victory marked a milestone for the FMLN, which began as a coalition of leftist guerrilla groups during El Salvador’s 12-year civil war. After the 1992 peace accords, the movement transformed itself into a political party and gradually built electoral strength, culminating in Funes’ win over the long-ruling conservative ARENA party.

Unlike some senior FMLN figures, Funes was not a combatant during the war. His background as a well-known broadcaster helped him appeal to moderate voters uneasy about the party’s revolutionary roots. His running mate, Salvador Sánchez Cerén, is a former guerrilla commander and veteran FMLN leader.

Analysts said the pairing reflected both continuity and change.

“Funes gave the FMLN a broader, more moderate face,” said a Central America political analyst. “But the expectations from the party’s traditional base are very high. He will have to balance pragmatism with the demands for deeper social change.”

During the campaign, Funes promised to fight poverty, expand health care and education, create jobs and reduce the country’s dependence on remittances sent home by Salvadorans living abroad, particularly in the United States. He also pledged to maintain close relations with Washington, a key partner for trade, migration and security.

“We are not here to dismantle what works,” Funes said during the campaign. “We are here to change what has failed.”

But the new president takes office facing severe economic challenges. El Salvador has been hit hard by the global financial crisis, with exports slowing, remittances declining and unemployment rising. The country uses the U.S. dollar as its currency, limiting the government’s ability to respond through monetary policy.

Business leaders have urged Funes to reassure investors and avoid abrupt economic shifts.

“What the country needs now is stability, confidence and clear rules,” said an official with a Salvadoran business association. “There is room for social investment, but it must come with fiscal responsibility.”

Public security is another urgent concern. El Salvador has one of the highest homicide rates in the region, driven by gang violence, organized crime and weak institutions. Funes has promised to strengthen law enforcement while also investing in prevention programs aimed at young people.

International officials welcomed the peaceful transfer of power as a sign of democratic maturity in a nation still shaped by memories of war.

“This is an important day for El Salvador,” said a regional diplomat attending the ceremony. “It shows that former adversaries can compete democratically and that political change can happen through institutions.”

For many FMLN supporters gathered in the capital, the inauguration was emotional. Some waved red party flags, while others carried photos of Archbishop Óscar Romero, the slain Catholic leader whose assassination in 1980 helped propel the country into civil war.

Funes invoked Romero in his speech, saying his administration would place the poor at the center of public policy.

“Our first commitment is to those who have waited the longest,” Funes said. “The forgotten will no longer be invisible.”

Still, the new government will be tested quickly. Funes must manage expectations from leftist supporters while maintaining confidence among business leaders, international lenders and the United States. He has signaled that his administration will pursue a moderate path, rejecting comparisons to more confrontational leftist governments in the region.

Analysts said his success may depend less on ideology than on results.

“The symbolism of this inauguration is enormous,” said one political observer. “But Salvadorans will judge Funes by whether he can improve daily life — jobs, security, schools, hospitals. The honeymoon may be short.”

As the ceremony ended, supporters outside the venue cheered and chanted Funes’ name, celebrating a moment many believed would never come: the FMLN, once an armed insurgency, now leading El Salvador’s government.

**El Salvador’s First Leftist President Takes Office, Ending Two Decades of ARENA Rule**

**SAN SALVADOR, El Salvador** — Mauricio Funes, a former television journalist whose election ended 20 years of conservative rule in El Salvador, was sworn in Monday as the country’s first leftist president, marking a historic turn for a nation still shaped by the legacy of civil war.

Funes, 49, took office before a crowd of regional leaders, foreign dignitaries and thousands of supporters in the capital, San Salvador, promising to govern with moderation while expanding social programs for the poor. His inauguration completed the transformation of the Farabundo Martí National Liberation Front, or FMLN, from a Marxist guerrilla movement into a democratic governing party.

“This is the beginning of a new era,” Funes told supporters, pledging to build “a government of national unity” and to address poverty, unemployment and crime in one of Latin America’s most densely populated countries.

Funes defeated Rodrigo Ávila of the right-wing Nationalist Republican Alliance, or ARENA, in the March presidential election, giving the FMLN its first national victory since El Salvador’s 1992 peace accords ended a 12-year civil war. ARENA had governed continuously since 1989, overseeing postwar reconstruction and close relations with Washington, but it faced growing public frustration over violent crime, rising living costs and persistent inequality.

The new president has sought to distance himself from fears that an FMLN government would follow the more confrontational socialist model of Venezuelan President Hugo Chávez. Instead, Funes has said he intends to pursue pragmatic policies, maintain strong ties with the United States and stabilize an economy heavily dependent on remittances from Salvadorans living abroad.

Funes takes office at a difficult moment. El Salvador’s economy has been battered by the global downturn, with exports weakening and remittances from the United States declining. The country also faces one of the highest homicide rates in the hemisphere, driven by gangs, organized crime and weak public institutions.

In his campaign and inaugural remarks, Funes promised a series of social initiatives aimed at easing poverty and expanding opportunity. His proposals include free school supplies and uniforms for children from low-income families, expanded health care access, support for small farmers, public investment to create jobs, and programs for vulnerable communities. He has also pledged to strengthen public security while improving police professionalism and crime prevention efforts.

The symbolism of the day was striking in a country where the FMLN once fought U.S.-backed governments during a brutal Cold War-era conflict that left about 75,000 people dead. The war pitted the Salvadoran military and allied right-wing forces against leftist guerrillas who accused the government of repression and exclusion. The conflict was marked by massacres, death squad killings and human rights abuses, including the 1980 assassination of Archbishop Óscar Romero and the 1989 murders of six Jesuit priests, their housekeeper and her daughter.

The 1992 peace accords disarmed the FMLN and turned it into a political party. Over the next two decades, the former rebels gained influence in municipal and legislative elections but repeatedly fell short in presidential contests. Funes, who was not a wartime commander, helped broaden the party’s appeal to centrist voters and business groups wary of the FMLN’s revolutionary past.

His running mate, Salvador Sánchez Cerén, is a former guerrilla commander and senior FMLN figure, underscoring the coalition Funes must manage between moderates and the party’s traditional left wing.

Outgoing President Antonio Saca, an ARENA member, handed over power peacefully, a transition hailed by observers as evidence of El Salvador’s democratic consolidation. In attendance were leaders and representatives from across the region, including officials from the United States, which remains deeply tied to El Salvador through trade, migration and security cooperation.

More than 2 million Salvadorans are believed to live in the United States, and remittances they send home are a critical source of income for families and the national economy. Funes has said he will advocate for Salvadoran migrants and seek continued cooperation with Washington, particularly on economic development and crime-fighting.

“We will be a respectful partner with all countries,” Funes said during the campaign, signaling that his government would not break with El Salvador’s dollarized economy or its free-trade commitments.

Still, expectations among FMLN supporters are high. Many see Funes’ victory as a long-delayed chance to address the social inequalities that helped fuel the civil war. In poor neighborhoods and rural communities, voters have called for better schools, clinics, jobs and protection from gang violence.

Political analysts say Funes’ challenge will be delivering change without alarming investors or deepening political polarization. His government will have to negotiate with a divided legislature and manage pressure from both the private sector and FMLN activists demanding more aggressive reforms.

For many Salvadorans, however, the inauguration represented a milestone unthinkable during the war years: a former rebel movement assuming power through the ballot box.

As FMLN flags waved in San Salvador and supporters chanted Funes’ name, the new president framed his election as proof that El Salvador had moved beyond armed conflict.

“The people have chosen hope,” he said. “Now we must turn that hope into results.”

**Funes Takes Office in El Salvador, Facing Poverty, Crime and a Divided Nation**

*San Salvador* — Mauricio Funes was sworn in Monday as president of El Salvador, ending two decades of conservative rule and bringing the former leftist guerrilla movement, the Farabundo Martí National Liberation Front, to power for the first time in the country’s history.

Funes, a former television journalist, assumed office amid high expectations from supporters who see his victory as a turning point for one of Latin America’s most unequal and politically polarized countries. But his administration begins under difficult conditions: widespread poverty, strained public finances, rising organized crime and lingering divisions from El Salvador’s 12-year civil war.

In his inaugural message, Funes pledged to govern for all Salvadorans, not only for the FMLN voters who carried him to victory. He faces the challenge of reassuring business leaders and conservative opponents while meeting the demands of poor communities that expect rapid improvements in jobs, security, health care and education.

El Salvador remains deeply divided between supporters of the FMLN and the right-wing Nationalist Republican Alliance, or ARENA, which governed from 1989 until this year. Those divisions are rooted in the civil war, which lasted from 1980 to 1992 and left more than 75,000 people dead. The FMLN began as an umbrella coalition of Marxist-inspired guerrilla organizations fighting U.S.-backed governments and military forces. After the 1992 peace accords, it disarmed and became a political party, gradually building electoral strength until Funes’ victory.

Unlike many of the FMLN’s historic commanders, Funes did not fight in the guerrilla movement. His moderate profile helped broaden the party’s appeal, particularly among urban voters and Salvadorans wary of radical change. During the campaign, he promised social programs and a more active state while insisting he would respect private property, maintain relations with the United States and avoid ideological confrontation.

One of the new president’s most immediate tests will be fiscal reform. El Salvador’s government has limited tax revenue and growing social needs, a situation worsened by the global economic downturn and the country’s dependence on remittances from Salvadorans living abroad, especially in the United States. Funes has signaled that he will seek to strengthen public finances, combat tax evasion and make the tax system more progressive, but any reform is likely to meet resistance from business groups and opposition lawmakers.

Poverty remains one of the country’s central problems. Many Salvadorans work in the informal economy or rely on money sent home by relatives overseas. Rural communities and urban neighborhoods alike face unemployment, inadequate public services and limited opportunities for young people. Funes has promised targeted anti-poverty measures, expanded health care and education programs, and assistance for families hit hardest by the economic crisis.

Security may prove even more urgent. El Salvador has one of the highest homicide rates in the region, driven by gangs, drug trafficking, extortion networks and organized crime. The growth of transnational criminal groups has strained police and judicial institutions, while ordinary citizens report living under constant threat in many neighborhoods. Funes has vowed to confront crime while also addressing the social conditions that feed gang recruitment.

His presidency marks a historic moment for the FMLN, but also a transformation for the party itself. Once a guerrilla army, it now controls the executive branch through elections and must prove it can govern a country with fragile institutions, limited resources and competing political pressures.

For supporters gathered in San Salvador, Funes’ inauguration represented hope after years of exclusion. For critics, it raised questions about the direction of the country under the former rebels’ banner. For Funes, the task ahead is to bridge those fears and expectations — and to show that El Salvador’s first leftist government can confront poverty, reform the state’s finances and restore security without deepening the national divide.

# Mauricio Funes sworn in as El Salvador’s first leftist president

**SAN SALVADOR, El Salvador —** Mauricio Funes, a former television journalist backed by a party once known for armed struggle, was sworn in Monday as El Salvador’s first leftist president, marking a historic political shift in a country long governed by the right.

Funes, 49, took office before regional leaders, foreign dignitaries and thousands of supporters gathered in the capital, ending two decades of rule by the conservative Nationalist Republican Alliance, or ARENA.

His victory brought the Farabundo Martí National Liberation Front, known as the FMLN, to power for the first time since it transformed from a guerrilla movement into a political party after El Salvador’s 12-year civil war.

“This is the most important day of my life,” Funes told the crowd, calling his inauguration a mandate for change. He pledged to govern “for all Salvadorans” and said his administration would seek reconciliation, social justice and economic recovery.

## From guerrilla movement to governing party

The FMLN was formed in 1980 as a coalition of leftist guerrilla groups fighting U.S.-backed Salvadoran governments during a civil war that left an estimated 75,000 people dead. The conflict ended with U.N.-brokered peace accords in 1992, after which the FMLN laid down its arms and became a legal political party.

For years, the party remained a powerful opposition force but fell short in presidential contests, often viewed with suspicion by business leaders and conservatives who warned that an FMLN government could steer El Salvador toward the model of Venezuela’s Hugo Chávez.

Funes sought to counter those fears throughout his campaign, presenting himself as a moderate social democrat inspired more by Brazil’s Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva than by more confrontational leftist leaders in the region.

In his inaugural address, Funes emphasized national unity and democratic institutions, saying the country was beginning “a new era” after years of inequality and political polarization.

He also promised to maintain strong ties with the United States, home to more than 2 million Salvadorans and the source of billions of dollars in annual remittances.

## A difficult economy from day one

Funes assumes office at a particularly challenging moment. El Salvador’s economy, one of the most dollarized and U.S.-dependent in Latin America, has been battered by the global financial crisis.

Remittances from Salvadorans living abroad — a lifeline for many families — have fallen as migrants in the United States lose jobs or see their incomes shrink. Exports and investment have also weakened, while poverty and unemployment remain persistent concerns.

The new president has promised expanded social programs, including assistance for poor families, school supplies for children and greater access to health care. But economists say his room to maneuver may be limited by slow growth, tight public finances and pressure to maintain investor confidence.

El Salvador uses the U.S. dollar as its official currency, which helps reduce exchange-rate risk but limits the government’s ability to use monetary policy to respond to downturns.

Analysts say Funes will face a delicate balancing act: satisfying the expectations of FMLN supporters who want deeper social change while reassuring markets, business groups and foreign partners that his government will remain fiscally responsible.

## Crime and migration remain central issues

Beyond the economy, Funes inherits one of the highest crime rates in the region. Gang violence, extortion and weak public security have long undermined daily life and business activity in El Salvador.

The new administration has promised to address insecurity through both policing and prevention programs aimed at young people vulnerable to gang recruitment.

Migration will also remain a defining issue. Many Salvadoran families depend on relatives working in the United States, and any changes in U.S. immigration enforcement or labor conditions could have immediate consequences at home.

## A symbolic turning point

For supporters packed into San Salvador, Funes’ inauguration represented more than a change in government. It was the culmination of a political transformation that began with the end of the civil war and the FMLN’s transition into electoral politics.

Funes, who was not a guerrilla commander during the war, has often been seen as a bridge figure — acceptable to the left’s historic base while less polarizing to centrist voters.

Still, expectations are high.

In his speech, Funes acknowledged the scale of the task ahead, saying his government would confront poverty, exclusion and the economic crisis without abandoning democratic principles.

“El Salvador has changed,” he said, promising a government rooted in hope, inclusion and respect for the rule of law.

For the first time, the former rebels of the FMLN now hold the presidency. The question facing Funes is whether a historic political victory can be translated into economic stability and meaningful improvements for a population still waiting for the promises of peace to be fully realized.
